sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of a federal witness-protection law. The core issue is the required mental state for a conviction.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 23, lines 51-35

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on March 29, 2011.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-17

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to require proof that the killer specifically intended to stop a federal report.
The government wants the Court to accept that the killer only needed to know the victim would report a federal crime.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 23, lines 51-35
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 19-41

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the statute demands a specific intent to prevent communication with a federal officer.
The government argues the statute protects federal investigations by punishing acts that hinder witness cooperation.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 23, lines 51-35

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if realistic likelihood of reporting proves the killer's intent to prevent that report.
Justice Alito asked if the statute focuses solely on the defendant's intent to prevent communication.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the mental state required for federal witness-protection charges. It clarifies the boundary between general criminal intent and specific federal intent. The outcome shapes how prosecutors prove intent in witness-interference cases. It impacts the scope of federal criminal jurisdiction over witness killings.
